title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rewriting it
dek: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation right, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
why: A 12-year hardware company's founder on the concrete mechanics of org rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs land — with details and the pits he fell into.
who: Founders, HR leaders and business owners pushing an AI org transformation, especially at hardware or consumer-electronics companies who want to move the org but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native org is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original org and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes; it's tearing them down first and rebuilding. He concedes this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: The HARO lead comes from tech, not HR
points.body: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not ordinary HR+IT: the lead must understand the business, and he picked an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person leads, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will do Agent Builder work) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people in the short term
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: Agent Builder leans technical, able to build an Agent; the FDE has to go into the business front line and map supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead they have business people spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their business work. The company also set an AI proficiency ladder from L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI 起航员’ (AI navigator) and above that ‘领航员’ (pilot).

points.h: Circles erase functional power; circle leads hold the bonus pool
points.body: Lockin's circles differ from project teams and Huawei's matrix: a matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team around an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — while HR and functional departments only have a right to advise. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within the first half-year to a year of the change the front line calls the shots.

Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear of doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the worst are the half-baked — whose experience hasn't arrived but who feel very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematized thinking as their foundation, but a clear-headed person judges more easily which processes and which roles can be removed. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skills and the ability to build Agents; only L3 can author workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits transformation speed varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and higher bonuses. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not raise quality, and 60-point output doesn't stick. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content drives conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, then sit down again
points.body: Lockin ran three internal rounds of sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as a dozen or so company-level Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content-marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting minutes and talks for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results were very good.

points.h: Hiring requires proving AI can't do the job
points.body: After a circle picks off people from an original department, the boss who wants replacements logically has only two channels: find AI management trainees, or use more AI tokens. If he really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and he has to explain why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end and are already near 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR or CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

Chen Bin says inside the company he is in fact the most radical one, often held back by everyone urging caution. On accumulations like Huawei's IPD, his judgment is: AI can only remake processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, SP to BP, from strategy to execution, used to take three months to half a year, now two months — double the efficiency — but the nodes like Five Looks Three Fixes remain, just three weeks becoming three days. Training a product-line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five, but the rotations that must happen can't be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk-tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, so you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature and then choose, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically notes that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk-tea shops are channel- and operations-driven, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user end to the supply-chain end, so it matters more there.

quotes.text: I think an AI-native org probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, as far as possible don't let a person do it. Think with AI-native thinking first, and even this process should logically be rebuilt.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm an end-to-end value-loop small team, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries — make the functional power smaller and the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it — but the half-baked ones are scary: their experience hasn't arrived, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

As far as possible we fill it with AI, right? Prioritize AI — whatever AI can fill, let AI fill it. Unless it can't be filled, and if it can't, then internally we say: either you say you'll fill it with AI management trainees, or you use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least double the efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed — it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, now it's three meetings, two meetings.

Look at the real value AI brings in this industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings, indeed a bit lower; and if it's lower, then you can, as it were, wait until these — people like us who are digging pits and playing around, right? — or until things like Doubao and Volcano Engine are done well, and then you just choose.
